3.title: Knowing Christ: The Surpassing Worth and the Pressing Forward
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is a warning and a testimony. Travelling teachers, Jewish Christians, were telling Gentile believers that faith in Christ was not enough: to belong fully to God’s people they must also be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Paul had fought this battle in Galatia and Antioch (Galatians 2; Acts 15), and he expects it to reach Philippi. His answer is his own life story. If anyone could have earned God’s approval by pedigree and performance, it was Saul of Tarsus: circumcised on the eighth day, a Benjamite, a Pharisee, zealous to the point of persecuting the church, blameless in the law. All of it he now counts as loss, even as dung, compared with knowing Christ and being found in him with a righteousness that comes from God through faith.

Then he guards against the opposite error. Having this righteousness does not mean you have arrived. Paul has not reached perfection; he presses on like a runner, forgetting what lies behind, because Christ has already taken hold of him. He warns of people who live as enemies of the cross, ruled by their appetites, and reminds the Philippians, proud citizens of a Roman colony, that their real citizenship is in heaven. From there they await a Saviour who will transform their weak, ageing bodies to be like his glorious body.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Everything I Had, and What It Was Worth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And now, my friends, rejoice in the Lord. I do not mind repeating myself; it keeps you safe. Watch out for those dogs, those evil workers, those mutilators of the flesh. For we are the true circumcision, we who worship by God’s Spirit, boast in Christ Jesus, and put no confidence in human achievement. I could, if anyone could. Circumcised on the eighth day, an Israelite of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew born of Hebrews; in the law a Pharisee; in zeal a persecutor of the church; in law-keeping righteousness, faultless. But whatever was profit to me I have written off as loss for Christ. In fact I count everything as loss next to the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. For him I have lost it all and count it as dung, so that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not with a righteousness of my own from the law, but the righteousness that comes from God through faith in Christ. I want to know him, the power of his resurrection and the fellowship of his sufferings, being shaped to his death, so that somehow I may reach the resurrection from the dead.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification: A Righteousness From Outside

Verse 9 is among the clearest statements of justification in the New Testament, and its decisive word is own. Paul does not say his law-righteousness was insufficient, or that he needed more of it; he has just called himself blameless. He says he does not want it — it is the wrong kind of thing. A righteousness of one’s own can produce only two outcomes, and both are fatal: if you believe you have achieved it, it makes a Pharisee, and Paul has shown you what that produced in him; if you know you have not, it crushes you.

Against it stands a righteousness that comes through faith and from God — faith being the channel and not the achievement, the beggar’s open hand rather than the coin. This is what the Reformers meant by imputation: Christ’s record credited to those who are in him. Luther called it an alien righteousness, alien not because it is strange but because it comes from outside — which is exactly its comfort. A standing that rests on his record is the same on your worst day as on your best, and will be the same on the day you are found in him.

Verse 11 should not be read as doubt. The man who has written that to die is gain and that departing is far better is not privately unsure whether he will be raised. “By any means possible” is openness about the route, not uncertainty about the destination.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Judaizers offered the Philippians a supplement — faith plus circumcision, grace plus performance. Paul’s answer is autobiographical and devastating: I held the complete set, more of it than any of you, and beside Christ it went out with the kitchen refuse. Note that this is not a man who found his old life worthless and therefore turned to Christ. It runs the other way. Everything on that list was real gain; he met something beside which it could not hold its value. Carry a lamp outdoors at noon and you would set it down and forget it, and nothing has happened to the lamp.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you is no trouble to me and is safe for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And so, my brothers and sisters, rejoice in the Lord. I do not mind writing the same things to you again; it is a safeguard for you.

Finally? “Finally” does not mean he is finishing; there are two chapters to go. The phrase (to loipon) means “as for the rest”, “and so”: a hinge to a new subject.

A command to rejoice. You cannot order someone to feel happy. But the command is not “be cheerful”; it is “rejoice in the Lord”. It gives joy an object. What can be commanded is where you look. Paul’s circumstances are a cell and a capital charge; the church has a quarrel; enemies are coming. Joy in the Lord is not a conclusion drawn from your situation but the place you stand while facing it.

Repetition is safe. Asphales: secure, a firm foothold. Teachers fear being boring. Paul does not. The truths we most need are not new; they are the same few, repeated, because we forget. Repetition is the handrail on the stair.

On a Tuesday. When the same Bible verse turns up again in a sermon or in your reading, do not think “I know that.” Think, “I needed that again.” Ask: where is my joy resting today, on my circumstances or on the Lord?

verseByVerse.quote: Look out for the dogs, look out for the evildoers, look out for those who mutilate the flesh. For we are the circumcision, who worship by the Spirit of God and glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watch out for the dogs, watch out for the evil workers, watch out for those who mutilate the flesh. For we are the true circumcision: we who worship by the Spirit of God, boast in Christ Jesus, and put no confidence in the flesh.

Who are they? Most likely Jewish Christian teachers who insisted that Gentile converts be circumcised, the same group Paul fought in Galatia (Galatians 5:2–12; Acts 15:1). Some think he means non-Christian Jews of the synagogue, but “evildoers” (literally “bad workers”) suggests rival missionaries who claimed to be working for God. Verdict: Judaizing Christians, whose “gospel” was faith plus law.

Dogs. Not pets. In the ancient Near East dogs were half-wild scavengers on the rubbish heaps outside towns, unclean animals. “Dog” was the usual Jewish insult for Gentiles, the outsiders. Paul turns it round: those who insist Gentiles must become Jews to belong are themselves the outsiders.

Mutilators. A pun that does not survive into English. Circumcision is peritomē, “cutting around”. Paul calls their practice katatomē, “cutting to pieces”, the word for the pagan self-gashing the law forbade (Leviticus 21:5; 1 Kings 18:28). A sign cut off from what it signifies is no longer a covenant sign; it is just surgery.

We are the circumcision. Gentile believers in Macedonia, mostly uncircumcised, are the true covenant people. This is what Moses and the prophets already said: “Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart” (Deuteronomy 10:16), and “circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter” (Romans 2:29).

Has the church replaced Israel? Some Christians (dispensationalists) keep Israel and the church as two distinct peoples with separate promises; others speak of the church simply replacing Israel. Paul’s view is a third way: there is one people of God, the olive tree of Romans 11, and all who trust Christ, Jew and Gentile, belong to it. Jews are not excluded; they are still “beloved for the sake of their forefathers” (Romans 11:28), and welcome on the same terms as everyone. Verdict: fulfilment, not replacement or two peoples. The church is Israel as God always meant it to be, centred on the Messiah.

Three marks of the true people. Worship by the Spirit, not by ritual machinery. Boasting in Christ, not in ourselves. No confidence in the flesh: “flesh” here means anything about you that you could offer as a reason God should accept you (family, record, discipline, never having done anything disgraceful).

Harsh words? Is such language ever right for Christians? Jesus called false teachers a “brood of vipers” (Matthew 23:33). But both he and Paul kept such words for those who corrupt the gospel and lead others astray, not for honest doubters or opponents in ordinary disputes. For the rest, “the Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone” (2 Timothy 2:24).

A textual note. The earliest manuscripts read “worship by the Spirit of God”. Some later ones read “worship God in the spirit” (KJV). The first is better attested and the harder, richer reading; it is original.

On a Tuesday. To find what your confidence rests on, notice what happens inside you when it is threatened. When your competence at work is questioned, or your reputation for being a good person takes a hit, do you feel your standing with God has moved?
verseByVerse.note: “Dogs” was a Jewish insult for Gentiles; Paul turns it on those insisting on circumcision. “Mutilate” plays on the word for circumcision. A pun: “those who mutilate the flesh” (katatomē) versus “the circumcision” (peritomē) in v. 3.

verseByVerse.quote: though I myself have reason for confidence in the flesh also. If anyone else thinks he has reason for confidence in the flesh, I have more: circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee; as to zeal, a persecutor of the church; as to righteousness under the law, blameless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not that I lack grounds for confidence in the flesh. If anyone thinks they have reason to trust in that, I have more. Circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, from the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew born of Hebrews; regarding the law, a Pharisee; regarding zeal, a persecutor of the church; regarding righteousness in the law, faultless.

Why the list. Paul will not let anyone say he despises what he never had. If this is a competition, he can win it.

Four inherited.

Circumcised on the eighth day: not a convert circumcised as an adult, nor an Ishmaelite circumcised at thirteen (Genesis 17:12, 25), but exactly as the law required.

Of Israel: the covenant people.

Of Benjamin: a proud tribe. It gave Israel its first king, Saul, whose name Paul bore; it stayed loyal to Judah and David’s line when the kingdom split; and Jerusalem lay on its border.

A Hebrew of Hebrews: though born in Tarsus, outside the land, he was raised in a family that kept the Hebrew (or Aramaic) language and ways, and he was educated in Jerusalem under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3).

Three achieved.

A Pharisee: the strictest, most respected party, devoted to keeping the law in detail. Not hypocrites as a class; many were deeply serious men.

A persecutor: zeal, after the pattern of Phinehas and the Maccabees, was proved by action against God’s enemies (Numbers 25:11). Paul lists his worst act as his best credential, because on the old accounting that is what it was.

Faultless: not sinless (compare Romans 7), but outwardly, publicly irreproachable. No neighbour could point to a broken rule.

The horror of it. This man kept the rules perfectly and was at the same time the chief enemy of God’s Son. Blamelessness had not made him good; it had made him dangerous. Religion without Christ can be a more effective barrier to God than open sin.

On a Tuesday. Write your own list: upbringing, church background, degrees, years of service, things you have never done. Then ask honestly whether any of it is a reason you expect God to accept you.
verseByVerse.note: Benjamin was the tribe of King Saul, Paul’s namesake. “Hebrew of Hebrews” may mean he was raised speaking Hebrew or Aramaic.

verseByVerse.quote: But whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ. Indeed, I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things and count them as rubbish, in order that I may gain Christ
verseByVerse.commentary:
But whatever was profit to me I have counted as loss because of Christ. More than that, I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. For his sake I have lost all things, and I consider them dung, so that I may gain Christ.

The ledger. Gain and loss are accountants’ words. Paul moves every asset to the other column. The same verb “count” appeared twice in chapter 2: Christ did not count equality with God as something to exploit (2:6); you are to count others more significant (2:3). Now Paul counts like Christ.

Three steps up. “I counted” (past: the Damascus road). “I count” (present: thirty years later, he still thinks so). “Everything” (the category widens from religious credentials to all things).

Rubbish. Skybala is a crude word: kitchen scraps thrown to the dogs, or excrement. The KJV’s “dung” is closer than the ESV’s “rubbish”. Paul has just called his opponents dogs; now he throws his own pedigree on the heap where dogs scavenge.

What it does not mean. Not that his heritage was bad. The covenant, the law and zeal for God were real gifts (Romans 9:4–5). The point is comparison. A lamp is precious at night; carried outside at noon, you put it down and forget it. Nothing is wrong with the lamp. Jesus told of a man who found treasure in a field, and “in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field” (Matthew 13:44). He did not feel he had given anything up.

My Lord. Paul rarely says “my Lord”. It is personal: not a doctrine but someone he knows.

On a Tuesday. Everyone in church says Christ is worth more than career or reputation. The test is what happened the last time one of those was threatened. Did it feel like putting down a lamp at noon, or like the end of the world?

For worship. Isaac Watts read these verses and wrote: “My richest gain I count but loss, and pour contempt on all my pride.”

verseByVerse.quote: and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith—
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I want to be found in him on the last day, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from keeping the law, but the righteousness that comes through faith in Christ: a righteousness from God, received by faith.

Found in him. On the day of Christ (1:6, 10; 2:16), at the final inspection, Paul’s whole hope is to be discovered inside someone else. Not standing next to Christ holding his own record, but in him, covered by his.

A righteousness of my own. The key word is “own”. Paul has just said he was faultless; he does not say his law-righteousness was too small. He says he does not want it. It is the wrong kind: a forged coin, not a small one. A righteousness of your own produces only two results. If you think you have it, you become proud. If you know you do not, you despair.

From God, through faith. Two prepositions. It comes from God: his gift, not our product. It comes through faith: faith is the channel, not the payment. The Reformers called this imputation: Christ’s record credited to my account because I am united to him. “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). Luther called it an “alien righteousness”: not strange, but from outside me. That is its comfort.

The New Perspective. Some scholars (E. P. Sanders, N. T. Wright and others) argue that first-century Judaism was not about earning salvation, and that “a righteousness of my own from the law” means Jewish covenant identity, the badges like circumcision that marked Israel off from Gentiles. There is truth here: Paul’s list does include badges of identity. But it also includes zeal and law-keeping, achievements, and he sets the whole lot against a righteousness that is God’s gift. Verdict: Paul is rejecting not just ethnic pride but any righteousness that is ours. The Reformation reading stands.

Faith in Christ or faithfulness of Christ? The Greek pistis Christou can mean “faith in Christ” or “the faithfulness of Christ”. Some modern scholars prefer the second: we are saved by Christ’s faithful obedience. That is true theology (2:8). But the verse goes straight on to say the righteousness “depends on faith”, which must be ours. Verdict: “faith in Christ”, as in the ESV, is the more natural reading.

On a Tuesday. When you have had a bad week, and failed in exactly the area you prayed about, your standing with God has not moved an inch. It rests on his record, not yours. Then get up and go on, not to earn it back, but because you already have it.

For worship. “Jesus, thy blood and righteousness / my beauty are, my glorious dress” (Zinzendorf, translated by John Wesley). Sing it to yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: that I may know him and the power of his resurrection, and may share his sufferings, becoming like him in his death,
verseByVerse.commentary:
I want to know him: to know the power of his resurrection, and to share in his sufferings, being shaped into the pattern of his death.

Know him. Not know about him, or know his benefits. Him. “Know” in the Bible is personal and covenantal: “You only have I known of all the families of the earth” (Amos 3:2). And this from an apostle of thirty years, who saw the risen Christ. Nobody knew Christ better, and nobody wanted to know him more.

Power and suffering, together. In the Greek they share one article: one thing with two sides. Paul puts resurrection first, out of chronological order, because that is how the Christian experiences it. We meet the risen Lord first, and his power is what makes suffering bearable. Nobody shares Christ’s sufferings in their own strength.

What it does not mean. Paul is not saying our sufferings add to Christ’s atoning work, which is finished (John 19:30). He means walking the same road as Christ: rejection, loss and self-giving for others (compare Colossians 1:24, 2 Corinthians 4:10).

Shaped to his death. One word, symmorphizomenos, built on morphē, “form”, the word of the hymn in 2:6–7. The pattern of Christ, who poured himself out, is being pressed into Paul. The tense is present: it is happening now, in a cell.

On a Tuesday. We often ask for resurrection power and rarely for fellowship in his sufferings. When a loss comes, a friendship ending because of your faith or a promotion missed because you would not cut a corner, it is not a detour from knowing Christ. It is one of the ways you come to know him.

verseByVerse.quote: that by any means possible I may attain the resurrection from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then, however God brings it about, I will reach the resurrection from the dead.

Doubt? “That by any means possible I may attain” sounds unsure. But this is the man who has just said to die is gain, that being with Christ is far better (1:21–23), and who will say in the next verse that Christ has made him his own. He is not unsure about the destination; he is open about the route. By a Roman sword or in an old man’s bed, by whatever road God chooses, he will go.

Certain, but not casual. The Bible holds together that God will keep you and that you must press on. Paul wrote both “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (1:6) and “I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified” (1 Corinthians 9:27). The certainty never produces a shrug.

Which resurrection? Literally “the out-resurrection from among the dead”. All the dead will be raised, the wicked too (John 5:28–29); no one need strive for that. Paul means the resurrection to glory, described in verse 21.

What it does not mean. Premillennial readers sometimes see here a special early resurrection of the faithful. Paul gives no hint of two stages; the phrase simply marks out the resurrection of those who belong to Christ.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) read “the resurrection of the dead”. The earlier and better reading is “from the dead”, which stresses rising out from among them.

On a Tuesday. If you are a Christian who does not know what the next year holds, cancer tests or a job interview, not knowing the road is not the same as doubting who waits at the end of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–16 — Not Arrived, and Still Running
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Not that I have already got there or been made perfect. I keep pressing on to take hold of it, because Christ Jesus has taken hold of me. No, friends, I do not think I have arrived. But one thing I do: I forget what is behind and strain towards what is ahead, and I run for the finish line, to win the prize of God’s upward call in Christ Jesus. All of us who are mature should think this way. And if on some point you see things differently, God will make that clear to you too. Only let us keep walking in line with what we have already reached.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sanctification Is Progress, Not Arrival

The Reformed tradition has always held that sanctification in this life is real but incomplete — the Westminster Confession speaks of it as imperfect in this life, with remnants of corruption abiding in every part. Verse 12 is the apostle’s own testimony to exactly that, and it is aimed at anyone claiming a settled plateau where striving is over.

The engine of the passage is the second half of verse 12: I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own. The same verb both times — to seize, to lay hold of. Paul chases Christ because Christ has already caught him on the Damascus road, while he was travelling the other way with warrants in his bag. Get that order wrong and the Christian life is unbearable: running in order to be apprehended is exhausting and never finished. Running because you were apprehended is another thing altogether, and it is why Paul can admit he has not arrived without the admission destroying him.

Verse 15 then supplies the paradox that defines maturity: the teleioi are precisely those who know they are not yet teleios. Anyone who believes he has finished has thereby proved he has not begun to think properly.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Some in the early church claimed a completed spiritual state, and Paul’s disclaimer is a direct correction of it. But note how he handles the difference in verse 15 — he does not repeat the argument louder or threaten. He hands them to God and expects God to do the persuading. That is patience, not indifference: he plainly thinks he is right and expects them to come round.

verseByVerse.quote: Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect, but I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own. Brothers, I do not consider that I have made it my own. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not that I have already obtained all this or already been made perfect. But I press on to take hold of it, because Christ Jesus has taken hold of me. Friends, I do not consider that I have taken hold of it yet. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and straining towards what lies ahead, I press on towards the finish line to win the prize: God’s call upward in Christ Jesus.

Not yet. After the loftiest sentences in the letter, Paul guards them. Some people claim a Christian can reach a plateau where the struggle is over. Paul, who had more right than anyone to claim it, refuses.

Can a Christian be perfect in this life? John Wesley taught “entire sanctification” or Christian perfection: a second work of grace after which the believer is free from wilful sin and loves God with an undivided heart. Holiness and some Pentecostal traditions developed it further. Wesley was not claiming sinlessness, and his concern for holiness was admirable. But Paul here, at the height of his maturity, denies having arrived. John writes to believers, “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8). Verdict: the Reformed view, that sanctification is real and growing but never complete before death or Christ’s return (Westminster Confession 13.2). Perfection is the goal, not a stage.

Because Christ took hold of me. The same verb twice, “to seize, lay hold of”. Paul runs to seize Christ because Christ has already seized him, on the Damascus road, while he was going the other way with arrest warrants (Acts 9). Running in order to be caught is exhausting. Running because you have been caught is joy.

One thing. A man with many churches, a trial and letters to write says his life has one thing in it.

Forgetting. Not amnesia; he has just listed his past in detail. It means not letting the past govern. Both ways: forget your failures (Paul had blood on his hands) and forget your successes (harder). A runner who looks back at either loses.

The race. The picture is the stadium. “Straining forward” is the runner’s body stretched towards the tape. The prize (brabeion) was the victor’s wreath. At the end of the Greek games the herald called the winner up to the judges’ stand to receive it. Here the call is from God, upward, to Christ himself. Compare Hebrews 12:1–2: “let us run with endurance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus”.

A textual note. A few early manuscripts (P46 and the Western text) add after “perfect” the words “or have already been justified”. It is a scribal addition, perhaps to rule out a misreading, and not original. Paul has just said in verse 9 that justification is a gift already received.

On a Tuesday. An elderly Christian who taught Sunday school for forty years still needs to press on. A new Christian with a dreadful past need not keep looking back at it. Both of you: face forward, eyes on Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The picture is of a runner straining toward the finishing line.

verseByVerse.quote: Let those of us who are mature think this way, and if in anything you think otherwise, God will reveal that also to you. Only let us hold true to what we have attained.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All of us who are mature should take this view. And if in some matter you think differently, God will make that clear to you as well. Only, let us live up to what we have already attained.

Mature and not perfect. “Mature” (teleioi) is the same root as “perfect” in verse 12, which Paul denied being. It is deliberate and a little wry. The mature are those who know they have not arrived. Anyone who thinks they have finished has not started thinking properly.

God will reveal it. One of Paul’s most gracious sentences on disagreement. Two paragraphs ago he called false teachers dogs; on the gospel itself he gives no ground. But on the outworking of the Christian life, where sincere believers see differently, he trusts God to do the persuading. He still thinks he is right (“that also”), but he is patient. Knowing which kind of question is in front of you is most of pastoral wisdom. Treat every disagreement as first-order and you will shred a church; treat none as first-order and you will lose the gospel.

Keep in step. Stoicheō: to walk in line, in rank. Whatever remains unclear, walk consistently in the light you already have.

A textual note. Later manuscripts add “let us walk by the same rule, let us mind the same thing” (KJV). The earliest manuscripts lack it; scribes probably filled it out from Galatians 6:16 and Philippians 2:2. Not original, but nothing in it is foreign to Paul.

On a Tuesday. When a fellow church member holds a different view on baptism, the end times or the gifts, and you have explained yours once, pray for them rather than argue again. Then keep obeying the light you both share.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–21 — Two Ways to Walk, and Where You Are From
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Friends, join together in following my example, and keep your eyes on those who live by the pattern we gave you. For many, as I have often told you and now tell you with tears, live as enemies of the cross of Christ. They are headed for destruction; their god is their stomach; their glory is in their shame; their minds are on earthly things. But our citizenship is in heaven, and from there we eagerly await a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ. By the power that enables him to bring everything under his control, he will transform our humble bodies so that they will be like his glorious body.
verseByVerse.theology:
Citizenship, and a Body That Will Be Raised

The noun in verse 20 is politeuma, sister to the verb Paul used at 1:27 when he told them to live as citizens worthy of the gospel. He planted it there; here is the flower. And the picture is not evacuation. A Roman colonia — which is exactly what Philippi was, settled with discharged legionaries and granted the standing of Italian soil — was not a party of homesick expatriates waiting for a boat. It was Rome made visible on the frontier. Heavenly citizenship does not license withdrawal from the city; it tells you what you are doing there. Note too that Soter and Kyrios were both Caesar’s titles, said in a town full of men who had sworn him an oath.

Verse 21 completes the pattern of the chapter 2 hymn and turns it on us. There Christ took the form of a slave; here the body of our humiliation — the noun is the one behind “he humbled himself” in 2:8 — is conformed to his body of glory. Against the Greek assumption that salvation means the soul escaping the body, Paul insists the body is not the problem and will not be discarded but changed: the same body made glorious, as Christ’s risen body was recognisably his own and still bore the wounds (John 20:27). And the guarantee runs from greater to lesser — the power that will subject all things to him is the power that will be applied to your body.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: “Join in imitating me” was said to people with no New Testament and no Christian upbringing, for whom the gospel had to be seen before it could be copied — and it was said by a man who had just admitted he had not arrived.

Now: Verse 21 is a word for the one who is ill, or ageing, or watching a body they love fail. What you live in now is the body of humiliation. It is not the last word about you.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, join in imitating me, and keep your eyes on those who walk according to the example you have in us. For many, of whom I have often told you and now tell you even with tears, walk as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame, with minds set on earthly things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Friends, join in following my example, and watch those who live by the pattern we set you. For, as I have often told you and now tell you even with tears, many live as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is their appetite, they take pride in what should shame them, and their minds are set on earthly things.

Imitate me? It sounds arrogant. Three things answer it. First, Paul means “as I am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1): he is a signpost. Second, the Philippians had no New Testament and no Christian upbringing; the gospel had to be seen before it could be copied. They had seen Paul flogged in their own city and singing at midnight in the jail (Acts 16:22–25). Third, the man saying “imitate me” has just said he has not arrived. He is not showing a finished product, but a direction.

And others. He widens it at once: watch anyone who lives this way. There is usually an old saint in your church worth watching more closely.

With tears. Paul weeps as he writes. That is the only posture from which to describe someone else’s ruin.

Who are the enemies of the cross?

Some think they are the Judaizers of verse 2: “their god is their belly” would then mean food laws, and “their shame” circumcision.

Most think they are professing Christians who turned grace into licence (libertines or antinomians), who said that because we are saved by grace it does not matter how we live (compare Romans 6:1; 16:18, “such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites”).

Verdict: the second. Paul calls them “many”, describes how they walk rather than what they teach, and contrasts them with the cross-shaped life of chapter 2. Having just warned against law-righteousness, he now warns against the opposite ditch. Both are enemies of the cross.

Four marks. Their end is destruction: Paul names the destination first. Their god is the belly: appetite on the throne, whatever in you says “I want”. They glory in their shame: boasting of what should embarrass them. Minds set on earthly things: the root of the rest, a mind with no horizon beyond this life.

On a Tuesday. A man who calls himself a Christian but boasts at the pub about his deals and his weekends is one of these. So, more quietly, is the person whose whole conversation is house prices, holidays and the next purchase. Pray for them with tears, not contempt, and check your own horizon.

verseByVerse.quote: But our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But our citizenship is in heaven, and from there we eagerly await a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ.

A colony. This verse explodes with meaning once you know Philippi. After the battle of Philippi (42 BC) and again after Actium (31 BC), Rome settled discharged soldiers there and made it a colonia with the “Italian right”: legally, its soil counted as Italian soil. Its citizens were Roman citizens, governed by Roman law, used Latin on their coins and inscriptions, and were proud of it. When Paul first came, the charge against him was teaching customs “not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice” (Acts 16:21).

Your capital is not Rome. Politeuma means a commonwealth or a body of citizens living abroad. Paul takes the proudest fact about their city and makes it a parable. You know what it is to live in Macedonia and belong to Rome. Now transpose it: you live in Philippi and belong to heaven.

What it does not mean. Not escape or withdrawal. A colony was not a group of homesick expatriates waiting for a boat home; it was Rome planted on the frontier so that Rome would be visible there. Heavenly citizens are the presence of heaven’s rule in their town. Neither does it mean we go up to heaven and stay there. The Saviour comes from heaven, to us, as the emperor might visit a colony.

Saviour and Lord. Both were imperial titles. Augustus and his successors were hailed as “saviour of the world” and “lord”. In a town full of veterans who had sworn an oath to Caesar, Paul gives both titles to Jesus.

Await. Apekdechomai: to wait eagerly, as someone watching the road for an arrival. One visible coming of Christ from heaven, the hope of the whole church, not a secret first coming and a later public one (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; Titus 2:13).

On a Tuesday. Ask: is there anything in how I spend money, time or ambition this week that would only make sense if Jesus were really coming back? A Christian who gives generously, forgives quickly or turns down a lucrative but crooked deal is living by the laws of another capital.
verseByVerse.note: Philippi’s citizens were proud to be citizens of Rome; believers belong to a heavenly commonwealth.

verseByVerse.quote: who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body, by the power that enables him even to subject all things to himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will transform our weak, humiliated bodies so that they share the form of his glorious body, by the same power with which he is able to bring all things under his rule.

The body of our humiliation. Literally that. The word is the noun of “he humbled himself” (2:8). Paul is not sneering at the body. He is naming what everyone over forty knows: these bodies tire, fail, forget, and are buried. Anyone who has watched a strong parent become unable to manage the stairs, or forget the names of their children, knows the phrase is not too strong.

A textual and translation note. The KJV’s “our vile body” is not a different text. In 1611 “vile” meant “lowly, of little worth” (from Latin vilis, cheap). It does not mean disgusting.

Transformed, not discarded. The Greek world mostly held that salvation meant the soul escaping the body. Paul says the body will be changed, not left behind. The same body made glorious, as Christ’s risen body was recognisably his and still bore the wounds (John 20:27). “It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory” (1 Corinthians 15:43). And “we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

The form again. “Like” is symmorphon, from morphē, the word of the hymn (2:6–7) and of verse 10. He took the form of a slave and our lowly body, so that we might share the form of his glory.

The guarantee. The argument goes from the greater to the lesser. The power that will put the whole universe under Christ, death included (1 Corinthians 15:25–27), is the power that will be applied to your body. If he can do the first, the second will not strain him.

On a Tuesday. A word for the one with dementia and the one caring for them; for the person in a wheelchair; for anyone at a graveside. What you see now is the body of humiliation. It is not the last word.

For worship. The chapter began with Paul throwing his pedigree on the rubbish heap and ends with the promise of a glorious body. Give thanks that what you lose for Christ is nothing next to what he will give, and that it includes you, body and soul.
